questions.q: A file upload vulnerability arises when a web server lets users upload files without sufficiently validating what?
choices: The file's name, type, contents, or size
Only the time of day of the upload
questions.explain: Failing to enforce restrictions on name, type, contents, or size can turn even a basic image upload into a way to place arbitrary, dangerous files on the server.

questions.q: In some cases, the act of uploading a file is itself enough to cause damage, without any follow-up request.
questions.explain: Sometimes uploading alone is damaging; other attacks need a follow-up HTTP request for the file, typically to trigger its execution.

questions.q: Failing to check that an uploaded file's size is within expected thresholds can enable which kind of attack?
choices: Denial of service by filling available disk space
questions.explain: An attacker can upload enough data to exhaust the server's disk, a form of DoS.

questions.q: If the filename is not validated properly, what can an attacker potentially do?
choices: Overwrite critical files by uploading a file with the same name
Force the browser to run JavaScript as root
questions.explain: A reused name can overwrite critical files; combined with directory traversal, files can even be written to unanticipated locations.

questions.q: How does a web server typically determine the type of a requested static file?
choices: It asks the client which type it wants
It parses the file extension and compares it to preconfigured extension-to-MIME-type mappings
It reads the entire file into memory and guesses
It uses the file's creation timestamp
questions.explain: The server parses the path for the extension and maps it to a MIME type; behavior then depends on the type and the server's configuration.

questions.q: On modern, dynamic websites the path of every request still maps 1:1 to the server's filesystem hierarchy.
questions.explain: Historically paths mapped 1:1 to files, but modern dynamic sites often have no direct relationship between request path and filesystem, though static files are still handled much the same way.

questions.q: If a requested file type is executable but the server is NOT configured to execute it, what commonly happens?
choices: The server returns an error or, in some cases, serves the file's contents as plain text
The browser is told to execute it client-side
questions.explain: Unconfigured executable types usually yield an error or get served as plain text, which can leak source code but nullifies a web shell.

questions.q: Which HTTP response header can hint at what kind of file the server thinks it served, often reflecting the extension/MIME mapping?
questions.explain: If not explicitly set by application code, Content-Type usually contains the result of the extension/MIME-type mapping.

questions.q: What is the term for a malicious script that lets an attacker run arbitrary commands on a remote server just by sending HTTP requests to the right endpoint?
questions.explain: A web shell gives effectively full control: reading/writing files, exfiltrating data, and pivoting to other systems.

questions.q: What does the PHP one-liner `<?php echo file_get_contents('/path/to/target/file'); ?>` do when requested?
choices: Returns the contents of a target file from the server's filesystem
questions.explain: Requesting the uploaded script returns the target file's contents in the response.

questions.q: Which web shell lets an attacker pass an arbitrary system command via a query parameter such as ?command=id?
questions.explain: system($_GET['command']) runs whatever command is supplied in the 'command' parameter, e.g. GET /exploit.php?command=id.

questions.q: Successfully uploading a working web shell effectively grants the attacker full control over the server.
questions.explain: With a web shell you can read/write arbitrary files, exfiltrate data, and pivot to internal and external systems.

questions.q: Why is trusting the part-specific Content-Type header of a multipart/form-data upload an insufficient defense?
choices: An attacker can freely set it (e.g. with Burp Repeater) while the actual file contents are unrestricted
It only appears for plain-text fields
questions.explain: If the server implicitly trusts the declared MIME type without checking that the contents match, the attacker just sets image/jpeg on a PHP file.

questions.q: Which content type is preferred for submitting large binary data such as an image or PDF in an HTML form?
questions.explain: x-www-form-urlencoded suits simple text; multipart/form-data splits the body into parts, each with its own Content-Disposition and optional Content-Type.

questions.q: JPEG files can be fingerprinted because they always begin with which byte sequence?
questions.explain: Checking header/footer signatures (JPEG begins with FF D8 FF) is more robust than trusting Content-Type, but still beatable with polyglots.

questions.q: Which tool is named for trivially creating a polyglot JPEG that hides malicious code in its metadata?
questions.explain: Even signature/dimension checks can be bypassed by embedding code in image metadata with ExifTool, producing a valid-looking JPEG that is also a script.

questions.q: Blacklisting dangerous file extensions is inherently flawed because it is hard to block every possible extension that could execute code.
questions.explain: Blacklists miss obscure-but-executable extensions such as .php5 and .shtml, and can be beaten with obfuscation.

questions.q: Which of the following are described techniques for obfuscating a file extension to slip past a blacklist? (Select all that apply)
questions.explain: Case tricks, multiple extensions, trailing chars/dots, URL-encoded or null-byte sequences, and multibyte unicode are all obfuscation tactics. The transport protocol is irrelevant.

questions.q: If a server strips the substring `.php` from the filename `exploit.p.phphp` but does not do so recursively, what remains?
questions.explain: Removing the inner .php from exploit.p.phphp leaves exploit.php, a valid executable extension.

questions.q: On an Apache server, which uploadable file could let an attacker map a custom extension to an executable MIME type, overriding global config?
questions.explain: Apache loads directory-specific config from .htaccess; if you can upload your own, you may map an arbitrary extension to an executable type even when the normal extension is blacklisted.

questions.q: On an IIS server, which file provides directory-specific configuration, such as adding a MIME mapping?
questions.explain: IIS uses web.config, e.g. a <staticContent><mimeMap .../></staticContent> directive to map an extension to a MIME type.

questions.q: Why might uploading a script to a directory not intended for user files lead to it being executed?
choices: All directories always run uploads as root
Execution configuration often differs between directories, and non-upload locations may lack the stricter controls
The browser caches and runs the script
Scripts outside the upload folder auto-compile
questions.explain: Upload directories usually have stricter controls; getting a script into a directory that is assumed out of reach of users may allow execution.

questions.q: Web servers often use which field in multipart/form-data requests to decide the name and location where an uploaded file is saved (enabling path traversal)?
questions.explain: Manipulating the filename field with ../ sequences can place a file in a directory where it will be executed.

questions.q: Sending all requests to a single domain name guarantees that one server with one configuration handles them.
questions.explain: A domain often points to a reverse proxy or load balancer, with requests handled by additional, possibly differently configured, back-end servers.

questions.q: How can a classic file-upload race condition arise?
choices: The server validates the file before the upload even starts
The file is written to the live filesystem and only removed after failing validation, leaving a brief window to execute it
Files are never written to disk at all
The antivirus runs before the upload completes
questions.explain: Sites that upload directly then delete on failure (common with AV scanning) leave the file present for a few milliseconds, which may be enough to request and execute it.

questions.q: If a temporary upload directory's randomized name is generated with PHP's uniqid(), why is that risky?
choices: uniqid() always returns the same value
The pseudo-random name can potentially be brute-forced
questions.explain: Because uniqid() is pseudo-random, the directory name may be brute-forced so the attacker can request the file before validation finishes.

questions.q: Uploading a larger file (payload at the start, followed by padding bytes) can lengthen the window for brute-forcing a randomized temp directory name.
questions.explain: If the file is processed in chunks, a larger file extends processing time, widening the race window.

questions.q: How do modern frameworks generally guard against these upload race conditions?
choices: By uploading to a temporary sandboxed directory with a randomized name, validating there, and only then moving the file to its destination
By running every uploaded file as root to test it
questions.explain: Battle-hardened frameworks avoid writing directly to the destination; they validate a randomized temp copy first. Hand-rolled processing is where race conditions tend to appear.

questions.q: If you can upload HTML files or SVG images, which client-side attack can you potentially launch with <script> tags?
questions.explain: An uploaded HTML/SVG file shown to other users runs its embedded script in their browser, a stored XSS.

questions.q: Because of the same-origin policy, an uploaded malicious client-side script works only if the file is served from the same origin to which it was uploaded.
questions.explain: If the upload is served from a different origin, same-origin policy restrictions prevent the client-side attack.

questions.q: Parsing of uploaded XML-based files such as .doc or .xls may be a vector for which attack?
questions.explain: If the server parses XML-based office files, it may be vulnerable to XML external entity (XXE) injection.

questions.q: Some web servers may be configured to support which HTTP method, providing an alternative way to upload malicious files even without an upload form?
questions.explain: PUT can upload a file directly if defenses are lacking. You can send OPTIONS requests to endpoints to find ones that advertise PUT support.

questions.q: It is recommended to check a file's extension against a whitelist of permitted extensions rather than a blacklist of prohibited ones.
questions.explain: Guessing which extensions to allow is far easier and safer than trying to enumerate every extension an attacker might try.

questions.q: Which of the following are recommended practices to prevent file upload vulnerabilities? (Select all that apply)
choices: Ensure filenames contain no directory or traversal sequences like ../
Rename uploaded files to avoid overwriting existing ones
Avoid writing files to the permanent filesystem until fully validated
Execute every uploaded file once to confirm it is safe
questions.explain: Strip traversal sequences, rename to prevent collisions, and defer permanent storage until validation passes. Executing uploads to 'test' them is exactly what you want to avoid.

questions.q: According to the prevention guidance, what should you do as much as possible instead of writing your own upload validation?
choices: Use an established framework for preprocessing file uploads
Store uploads in the web root
questions.explain: Writing your own validation is complex and error-prone (and can introduce race conditions); an established framework handles preprocessing more safely.
